title: Fan Fiction
bodyHtml:
MARY SU.0 is a fan-fiction writing robot. Fan fiction is a fiction written by people using another author's characters. Unfortunately, she's not very good at what she does. MARY writes fan-fiction by reading the text of a book (or series of books) and randomly generating new sentences based on the text. Her latest effort is fan-fiction based on the Harry Potter book series.

MARY SU.0 has a few different methods that she's able to use for generating sentences. The first class of methods are called n-gram methods. The simplest of these methods is the unigram method. In the unigram method, MARY chooses each token of the sentence completely randomly from the entire vocabulary of the book she read. (A token can also be a punctuation mark.) An example of a sentence generated using this method might look like this:

gave spiral the truly poisoned, Neville the shoulder Invisibility

A second method is the bigram method. In this method, MARY first finds all the tokens that were used to start a sentence in the text and randomly chooses one of these to start the sentence. Then she builds the rest of the sentence by looking at the most recent token generated, finding all tokens that occur immediately after that token in the text, and randomly choosing one of these. For example, if the most recently generated token was “red”, MARY would find all the tokens in the text that immediately follow “red”, {“hair”, “curtains”, “as”, …} and randomly choose one of these to be the next word. A sentence generated using the bigram method might look like this:

Face your nose noisily after you saying stuff.

A third method is called the trigram method. This method is very similar to the bigram method, but uses the previous two tokens (instead of the previous one) to decide what the next token will be. A sentence generated using the trigram method might look like this:

But Harry hardly noticed that six extra chairs.”

The last method that MARY can use to generate sentences is called the Context Free method. This method starts by taking each sentence in the text and generating a grammar tree, like the one below, for it.

The symbols that aren't words refer to labels of words or larger sequences. Some symbols refer to parts of speech, such as NNP for proper noun, PRP for personal pronoun, VBD for a verb in past tense, and TO for preposition. Other labels refer to sequences of words that form units, such as S for sentence, NP for a noun phrase, a sequence of one or more words that behaves like a noun (e.g. dogs or the big dogs), and VP for a verb phrase, which is a sequence of one or more words that behaves like a verb (e.g. goes or went to the store).

To generate a new sentence, she first generates an “S” which represents a sentence. Then she looks through her collection of grammar trees for all the sets of symbols ([NP VP .] for example) that occur immediately under an “S”. She then repeats this process recursively for each of the new items generated until the tree has no more nodes that can be expanded (once a token is generated, it cannot be expanded). A sentence generated by this method might look like this:

The next question will cast by Ron.

Headmaster uninjured could that was Malfoy that badges
He bent over top of the water blushing furiously.
There were crouching in your bedroom.
He lived about a hundred wizards were closing.
Ron spooned iron bolts, keyholes, and a heavy wooden breadboard on to her back and picked up a fistful.
"What?" said Harry.
‘Sorry!’ he said," said Mr. Malfoy's eyes.
Harry wasn't," said Dumbledore went slightly surprised.
years beginning at to annoyance spider!" just months Harry
You might have been an impostor.
They'll be the first to rise up in the Invisibility Cloak on," said Professor Flitwick pressed a box into his bag.
The broom gave them an enormous wink.

questions.promptHtml: a. Headmaster uninjured could that was Malfoy that badges
questions.partPrompt: Below is a collection of sentences. Two of them are real sentences from the Harry Potter series. The rest were generated using one of the methods above; each method generated at least two sentences. Write either "u" for unigram, "b" for bigram, "t" for trigram, or "c" for context-free to indicate the method that most likely generated that sentence, or if you think the sentence was not automatically generated, write "r" for real.

hints.text: Ask of each sentence: how far can you read before it stops making sense? A unigram sentence falls apart between any two neighbouring words, a bigram sentence holds together only two words at a time, a trigram sentence holds together three at a time, and a context-free sentence is grammatical all the way through even when it is silly.

The n-gram methods only ever see a short window of words, so their mistakes are long-distance ones: a sentence that starts one way and finishes as if it were a different sentence, or quotation marks and commas that open but never close. The context-free method builds a whole tree, so its output is always grammatical and its punctuation always balances; the only thing wrong with it is the meaning. Real sentences are grammatical AND sensible. Remember the counting constraint: exactly two are real and each of the four methods produced at least two, so the twelve split 2/2/2/2 plus two extras.

Try the method on the example printed in the problem: "Face your nose noisily after you saying stuff." Slide a two-word window along it - "Face your", "your nose", "nose noisily", "noisily after", "after you", "you saying", "saying stuff" - every pair is something you could hear in English, but no three-word stretch such as "after you saying" is, and the sentence as a whole has no coherent structure. That is the fingerprint of the two-word window, and it is why the problem labels this example a bigram sentence.

explanationHtml:
What each machine can and cannot see

All four of MARY's methods are random, but they differ in how much of the sentence they look at while choosing the next word. That “memory” is exactly what you can hear in the output.

  • Unigram: no memory at all. Every token, including punctuation, is drawn independently from the whole vocabulary. Even two words standing side by side will usually not fit together.
  • Bigram: memory of one word. Each neighbouring pair of words is something that really occurred in the books, so pairs sound fine, but stretches of three or more words normally do not.
  • Trigram: memory of two words. Now every three-word window really occurred in the books, so the text sounds almost natural in short bursts. The breakdowns are longer-range: the sentence slides from one original sentence into another wherever they shared a two-word overlap.
  • Context-free: no memory of words at all, but complete memory of structure. It builds a grammar tree top-down, so the result is always a well-formed sentence: subject, verb, matching quotation marks, a full stop in the right place. What goes wrong is the meaning, because the words are slotted into the tree with no regard for what they mean.
  • Real: grammatical and meaningful.

Three tests to apply

Test 1 - the sliding window. Read the sentence in chunks of two words, then three. If even the two-word chunks are nonsense (“Headmaster uninjured”, “beginning at”, “annoyance spider”), you are looking at a unigram. If the pairs are fine but no three-word stretch survives, it is a bigram. If three-word stretches sound like real English but the sentence as a whole changes horses in midstream, it is a trigram.

Test 2 - punctuation bookkeeping. The n-gram methods treat quotation marks and commas as just more tokens, so they happily produce a closing " with nothing opening it, or an exclamation mark in the middle of a line. The context-free method inherits the punctuation from the tree, so its punctuation is always tidy. Any sentence with an orphaned quotation mark was made by an n-gram method (or is a real line whose opening quote sits in the previous sentence - but the real ones here are self-contained).

Test 3 - does it mean anything? If the sentence is perfectly grammatical, well punctuated, and still absurd - a broom winking, someone spooning iron bolts and keyholes - that is the signature of the context-free method. If it is grammatical, punctuated, and plausible in a Harry Potter book, it is real.

Working the examples

Take There were crouching in your bedroom. Pairs: “There were”, “were crouching”, “crouching in”, “in your”, “your bedroom” - every pair is fine. Triples: “There were crouching” is not English, and neither is “were crouching in your bedroom” as a complete clause with “there”. One word of memory, no more: bigram.

Take He lived about a hundred wizards were closing. Now the triples are all real English: “He lived about”, “about a hundred”, “a hundred wizards”, “hundred wizards were”, “wizards were closing”. The machine started copying one sentence (“He lived about a hundred...”) and, at the two-word overlap “a hundred”, jumped into another (“...a hundred wizards were closing”). Two words of memory: trigram.

Take years beginning at to annoyance spider!" just months Harry. Nothing holds together even for two words, there is no capital letter at the start, no full stop at the end, and punctuation floats in the middle. That is a bag of words: unigram.

The broom gave them an enormous wink. is faultless English - NP, VP with a past-tense verb, an indirect object, a full stop - but brooms do not wink. Perfect structure, broken meaning: context-free. The same reasoning applies to the long sentence about spooning iron bolts and keyholes onto someone's back: grammatically it is a textbook compound predicate with a list, semantically it is nonsense.

Finally, "What?" said Harry. and You might have been an impostor. are short, grammatical, correctly punctuated, and could sit unnoticed on a real page. Those are the two real lines the problem promised, which is a useful check: exactly two must be real.

The counting check

The problem tells you two sentences are real and each of the four methods produced at least two. That is 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10 accounted for, leaving two extra sentences to be shared out. So if you find yourself assigning only one sentence to some method, or three real ones, go back and re-test the doubtful cases.
_reviewNotes:
Answer keys come from the official solution page, which prints the full method names (unigram, context-free, bigram, trigram, real). The booklet instructs students to write the single letters u/b/t/c/r, so the answerKey is stored as the letter with the full word as an accepted variant, and the letters are given as fixed choices; confirm this is the desired answer format.
Points: 10 official points spread evenly over 12 blanks (0.83/0.84 each).
